extracted.intended_audience: creative writers (poets and prose writers), podcast listeners learning word-choice and rhythm
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for poets and prose writers on treating words as objects — focusing on sound, shape, rhythm, and revision techniques to create stronger images and musicality in writing. Includes practical habits (journaling, reading aloud, substitution, cutting) and approach to form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pick the exact right word for shape/sound/visual space
rubrics_metrics.description: Picking the right exact word, for the shape, sound, visual space, as an object unto itself, independent of meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat words as objects; consider how a word looks on the page, how it feels in the mouth, and its sonic character in addition to meaning. Use substitution (soft vs hard words, sibilants vs popping consonants) to change flavor and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Taste your words; find rhythm and breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Taste your words, feel them, find the rhythm, the breaks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slow down and attend to each word to discover cadence. Identify natural breaks and emphasize them in revision and performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read poetry slowly — savor like a fine meal/wine
rubrics_metrics.description: “Poetry is to be read like a fine meal or a fine wine, one sip at a time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For poetic lines, avoid speed-reading; slow performance often reveals nuance and musicality that informs revision and composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep journals and capture everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals! Write down anything and everything, then go back and pull out words and ideas and feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a phone or small notebook to jot overheard lines, end-of-night thoughts, images. Later mine journals for seeds of poems or phrases to build into work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert between stories and poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Write stories and turn them into poems. Write poems and create stories out of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be flexible about form; a single sentence or scene can be reshaped into a poem or story depending on which words you remove or emphasize.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create poems by taking words out
rubrics_metrics.description: Take words out. Change words. ... With poetry, you’re creating an image with as few words as possible. An easy way to do that is you start taking words out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In revision, remove extraneous words (even the 'most important' ones) to open space and let readers supply meaning. Trimming creates shape and musical economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read drafts aloud to test sound and rhythm
rubrics_metrics.description: I always read them out loud. Because for me, that is where I can hear whether it’s working or not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use oral performance (cold readings of others' work and reading your drafts) to detect awkwardness, rhythm problems, or better word choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use surprising substitutions to shift image/effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace a soft word with a hard word (e.g., satin → razor) to create a startling image and shake up the mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiment with swapping words that differ in texture, consonant quality, or connotation to produce unexpected imagery or tonal contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play with sibilants vs bebop/pop consonants
rubrics_metrics.description: Change hard and soft words, or sibilants and bebop. ... taking a word that is full of sibilance ... replacing it with a word that’s full of b’s and popping, a bebop sort of word, has a completely different flavor in the mouth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consonant and vowel choices affect the oral 'flavor' of a line; use sound contrasts intentionally to support mood and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remove the most important word to invite reader participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Take out the most important word, and let the reader put their own ideas, their own breath, their own emotion in there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: removing 'life' from 'Some days life feels like...' creates ambiguity so readers can supply context, deepening engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leave space; avoid over-explaining (cut first/last stanza)
rubrics_metrics.description: When you write a poem, take out the first and the last stanza. Because we have a tendency to over explain. Take that out, and see what you have left.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim framing and exposition that telegraphs meaning; leave gaps for reader interpretation and emotional resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play with poetic rhythms and internalize forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Play with the rhythms of poetry, to learn them. Make them an unconscious rhythm that you can draw on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study forms (sonnets, haiku) and practice them so rhythm becomes an available tool. You don't have to write to the form every time, but learning forms builds an internal sense of cadence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mathematical/structural analysis of rhythm as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Michael Collins’ definitions and examples of forms ... are quite mathematical. Which is simply a way of defining the rhythms of a poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break down syllable counts and stress patterns analytically if useful; treating rhythm structurally can help design desired musical effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of character voice and vocabulary limits
rubrics_metrics.description: There are words that just don’t fit in character voice. Even though it’s the word that very much might best sell that punchline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose words consistent with character and context; if a needed word breaks voice, consider changing the scene or speaker rather than forcing the word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overusing the same words; expand choices
rubrics_metrics.description: I tend to use the same words, because those images… I do like to be aware if I’ve overused words, and use something entirely different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track repetitive word use (journals will reveal this). Deliberately seek fresh diction to avoid stale phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to form unconsciously — form communicates beyond meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Adhering to a form, even unconsciously, is effective for a reason. The form exists because it communicates things to us in a way that the meanings of the words don’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form to convey mood and expectation; even if you don't follow form strictly, its patterns influence reader response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry/music analogy — use musicality in storytelling
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry, like music, is organic and normal. It’s the cadence of storytelling around the fire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat lines as musical phrases; attention to tempo, beat, and phrasing enhances both poetry and prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be accessible; write what you feel first
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry does not have to be difficult. Especially when you’re just starting out. Write what you feel. Write what comes to mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin with honest notes and images; accessibility and emotional clarity are valid aims. Formal concerns can come later in revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice cold readings of others' work to focus on word-level detail
rubrics_metrics.description: I actually like to do cold readings of other people’s work because it makes me concentrate on each word, and I find a word can be quite delicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read unfamiliar poems aloud to sharpen sensitivity to diction, rhythm, and line breaks; treat it as an exercise in word-focused listening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use substitution and restructuring to place key words for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a word in a punchline, or in the last line of the comic, there is a word that I want to put as close to the end as possible. Which means structuring the sentence in a way that that word actually makes sense at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange sentence structure to position impactful words where they will have maximum emotional or comedic effect; restructure earlier phrasing if necessary.
